BPM Justification: Matching compute to demand for AI/ML training jobs is a core resource-efficiency lever; since the guideline explicitly frames this around 'workload processes,' I read it as shaping how the process-triggered training task is hosted and scaled, even though the process-modeling notation itself isn't addressed.
Shortening network distance is a straightforward energy-transmission win, but it's a placement decision made once for a deployment rather than something tied to a specific business process.
Better bin-packing of containers reduces embodied carbon across whatever workers happen to run in them, a solid infra-efficiency practice, though it isn't specific to any one task or process.
Stateless services can be right-sized and scaled far more precisely, one of the more reliable levers for cutting over-provisioned compute and its embodied carbon.

Smoothing out request spikes through queuing is a well-known energy-proportionality technique at the infrastructure/worker level; I don't see a strong tie to how a specific process is structured, more a generic buffering pattern.

Running inference at the edge cuts data-transfer energy and reliance on centralized compute, a meaningful carbon lever for any AI-backed service, even if the guideline is really about where a task's compute happens rather than about process design.

Independently scalable components avoid over-provisioning the whole system to satisfy one busy part, a solid efficiency pattern; the guideline is framed generically around microservices rather than around process-triggered tasks specifically.

Hardware/accelerator selection is one of the highest-leverage energy decisions for AI workloads; even though it's an infrastructure choice, I'd flag it as touching the backing task whenever that AI workload is invoked by a process step.

Eliminating idle compute by only running AI/agent workloads on demand is a strong, direct carbon-reduction pattern; I read the 'trigger only when needed' framing as describing worker/infrastructure behavior rather than the process model itself.
Evaluating ARM vs. x86 is a legitimate energy-efficiency lever at the hardware layer, but it's a one-time platform decision with no natural connection to any specific process.

Serverless sharing infrastructure across many tenants is a reliable way to cut idle capacity and embodied carbon; it's a hosting-model choice though, not something a process designer decides on a per-process basis.

A front-end presentation choice (fonts, system assets) with no meaningful energy story tied to how an organization runs its operations; even generously, I can't connect this to anything BPM would touch.

Rendering cost scales with DOM size, a real if small energy effect for any browser-based task UI a process might present to a user, though the guideline is squarely a front-end implementation concern.
Request-chain length affects page energy cost, a legitimate but narrow web-performance concern for whatever task renders the page.

Minimizing what gets tracked and stored is a direct data-minimization win with real energy and storage benefits; the same principle should apply to trimming any unnecessary variables or history a process carries.
Caching to avoid unnecessary remote reads is one of the most reliable energy-saving techniques available; it applies at the task/service level rather than being specific to a process.
Storage compression reduces both energy and embodied carbon from unnecessary capacity; this applies just as much to process documents and history as to any other stored data.
Transmission compression is a dependable network-energy win; it would reduce the cost of any data a process passes between its tasks or systems, even though the guideline itself is generic.
Lazy-loading images is a front-end rendering optimization with a real but very small energy footprint, and I can't tie it to any organizational process, even loosely.
A media-format substitution with a genuine bandwidth benefit, but it's a content-authoring decision with no link to how any organization's processes run.
Compressing HTTP text responses is basic, effective network-energy hygiene for any service, but it's a generic server configuration rather than something process-specific.
Reducing the number of page sub-resource requests helps page-load energy, but this is a front-end concern with no organizational-process story attached.

Reusing pre-trained models instead of training from scratch is one of the biggest compute/energy savings available in AI development; when that model backs an AI task invoked by a process, the efficiency gain carries straight through.
Offloading heavy computation off the main thread improves multi-core utilization and cuts energy waste, a real but browser-implementation-level concern.

Every extra environment (dev, staging, QA, etc.) multiplies embodied carbon and energy for no functional benefit; trimming environments is a straightforward, high-value sustainability lever across any organization's IT estate.

Cutting redundant model invocations through caching and conditional logic directly reduces the single biggest energy cost in agentic AI systems; since it's the orchestration layer itself being optimized, I see this as a core sustainability practice for any AI-driven workflow.

Efficient storage formats and indexing for AI datasets cut storage footprint and retrieval compute substantially; a strong sustainability lever, even though it lives inside a single training/inference task.
Right-sizing images saves bandwidth and storage, but it's a content-asset concern with no connection to organizational process operations.
Minimizing transmitted data size is a foundational network-energy practice; it would reduce the cost of any payload a process passes between tasks, though the guideline is stated generically.
Removing dead CSS reduces parsing overhead marginally, but this is front-end code hygiene disconnected from any process or organizational operation.
Framework/runtime choice can swing compute overhead significantly for ML workloads; a genuine sustainability lever, though it's an implementation detail of whichever task or service runs the model.
Modern image formats reduce bandwidth and compute, a real but content-asset-level win with no organizational-process tie.
Avoiding repeated TLS handshakes saves real CPU cycles and energy at scale, but it's squarely a network/security-infrastructure configuration decision.

Avoiding blocked threads on synchronous calls is a solid resource-utilization practice, but it's an implementation choice inside a task's calling code rather than something visible at the process level.

The energy gap between interpreted and compiled execution is one of the most well-documented findings in green software research; a real efficiency lever for whatever service backs a task, even though the choice is made once per service rather than per process.

Model right-sizing is arguably the single highest-leverage decision for AI energy consumption, and whenever that model is the backing implementation of an AI task invoked by a process, this guideline directly determines that task's carbon footprint.

Shifting rendering to the server and caching it reduces client-side energy at scale, a solid win for high-traffic pages, but this is a front-end architecture decision without a process-specific angle.
Orphaned storage keeps consuming energy and embodied carbon for zero benefit; cleaning it up is one of the simplest, highest-confidence sustainability wins in cloud operations.
Consolidating onto fewer, better-utilized VMs directly improves energy proportionality and reduces embodied carbon per unit of useful work, a core capacity-management sustainability practice.
Same energy-proportionality logic as VM consolidation: fewer, better-utilized servers reduce both operational energy and embodied carbon.
Maximizing storage utilization reduces both energy proportionality issues and embodied carbon from underused capacity, a solid general sustainability practice.

Average CPU utilization is one of the clearest levers for energy proportionality across a whole fleet; a fundamental efficiency practice even if it's applied at the infrastructure level rather than per process.
Reducing over-provisioning driven by peak load is a direct embodied-carbon reduction, similar in kind to average-utilization tuning.
Power/thermal management for constrained edge devices is a meaningful lever for the growing footprint of edge AI, though it's a hardware operations concern rather than a process-design one.
Idle cloud resources quietly accumulate energy use and embodied carbon; removing them is one of the most straightforward operational sustainability wins available.

Idle applications still consume CPU through background work, so scaling them down when unused is a solid, direct energy-waste elimination; I'd tie this to the worker/infrastructure layer rather than to process design specifically.
Turning off dev/test nodes outside office hours avoids clearly wasted energy, a specific but modest-scope tactic.
Matching infrastructure to actual demand is one of the most fundamental sustainability practices in cloud computing, avoiding underused/inefficient resources at scale.
Demand-based scaling on signals like queue length or HTTP load is a strong, well-established resource-efficiency pattern; framed generically around Kubernetes rather than around any specific process.
Automated deletion of aged data is a reliable way to keep storage's embodied-carbon footprint proportional to what's actually needed, a strong general data-lifecycle sustainability practice.

Shifting scheduled jobs to low-carbon-intensity windows is one of the clearest applications of carbon-aware computing; I read it mainly as an infrastructure-scheduling practice rather than a process-modeling decision.

Carbon-aware scheduling and region selection is the flagship practice in this whole field: choosing when and where compute runs based on grid carbon intensity is a direct, measurable, and often the single largest lever for reducing an AI workload's footprint.
Avoiding futile repeated calls to a dead dependency saves some wasted compute and network energy, a real but fairly modest-scale resilience pattern at the service level.

The guideline frames vulnerability scanning in terms of avoiding the embodied carbon of compromised infrastructure being misused; a secondary but real sustainability angle on a primarily security practice.
Blocking unauthorized traffic at the source does avoid some wasted transmission energy, though the sustainability case here is thinner and mostly a side effect of a security control.
Preventing floods of meaningless requests does avoid real wasted compute and network energy, though this is fundamentally a security control with sustainability as a secondary benefit.

Encryption has a real, measurable compute cost, so scoping it to only what's necessary is a legitimate efficiency practice; it would apply to whatever data a process carries, but the guideline itself is generic security advice.

Not over-engineering for maximal availability directly reduces the redundant infrastructure a service needs, a substantial and often underappreciated energy/carbon lever; I read this mainly as an infrastructure-provisioning consequence rather than an organizational-governance one.

Shedding low-priority requests under load or high grid-carbon-intensity avoids adding infrastructure and the emissions that come with it; a solid throttling/rate-limiting technique, though I read it mainly as an infra/service-level control rather than a process-design decision.
